protocol: Blind subject review: choose exactly one option per item, explain why, and flag ambiguity or a missing assumption. The author key and explanations have not been supplied.

items.prompt: An ideal uniform sampler records 20 samples per second. Its first sample has index n = 0 at t = 0. At what time is the sample with index n = 4 recorded?
A record contains exactly nine uniformly spaced samples at 40 samples per second, with indices 0 through 8. What is the elapsed time from the first recorded sample to the last recorded sample?

An acquisition was configured for 10 samples per second. A saved four-row excerpt records timestamps 0.0, 0.1, 0.2 and 0.4 seconds. The excerpt gives no reason for the timing. Which conclusion follows from these timestamps?
options: Every adjacent pair is 0.1 s apart because the configured rate was 10 samples per second.
The last timestamp should be replaced by 0.3 s because there are four rows.
The excerpt proves that exactly one physical measurement was lost during storage.
The last adjacent interval is 0.2 s; the nominal rate alone does not establish why.

items.prompt: Consider zero-phase, unit-amplitude cosine waves x(t) = cos(2π f t), with f in hertz. Sample at t = n/8 seconds for every integer n. Which other frequency gives exactly the same infinite sample sequence as f = 1 Hz?
The wave x(t) = cos(2π · 9t) is sampled uniformly at 12 samples per second, starting at t = 0. Which zero-phase, unit-amplitude cosine below 6 Hz has the same samples at every recorded index?
An exact sampler observes x(t) = sin(2π · 4t) at times t = n/8 seconds, where n is an integer. What sequence does it record? Assume no noise or timing error.
options: One complete visible sine-wave cycle every four samples.
Zero at every sample, although the continuous wave is not identically zero.

items.prompt: An otherwise arbitrary continuous signal is known to have no frequency components above 6 Hz in magnitude. Under the ideal theorem for a complete infinite sequence of exact uniform samples, which listed rate is strictly above twice that highest possible frequency?

An analog input may contain both a desired 3 Hz cosine and an unwanted 17 Hz cosine. It will be sampled at 20 samples per second. Which step prevents the unwanted component from becoming indistinguishable from a 3 Hz cosine in the samples? Assume the stated ideal filter is available.
options: Join the recorded samples with smoother curves.
Apply an analog low-pass filter before sampling that passes 3 Hz and removes 17 Hz.
After sampling, remove only the 17 Hz component from those samples while keeping every possible 3 Hz component.
Record more samples at the same rate and then identify the two components from the samples alone.

items.prompt: Only five exact samples of an otherwise unspecified signal are available. The signal is band-limited to 3 Hz and those samples came from an 8 samples/s uniform clock. Which statement correctly applies the usual ideal sampling theorem under only these assumptions?
options: The complete infinite uniform sample sequence would determine the band-limited signal; five values alone do not determine its entire waveform.
Those five values uniquely determine the entire waveform because 8 is greater than twice 3.
No amount of data at 8 samples/s can reconstruct a signal band-limited to 3 Hz.
The original waveform must equal the straight lines joining the five sample points.

items.prompt: Two exact recorded values are x(0 s) = 0 and x(1 s) = 2. A display uses linear interpolation and shows x = 1 at 0.5 s. No measurement was taken at 0.5 s and no rule for the between-sample signal was supplied. What is the status of the displayed middle value?
options: It is an additional physical measurement supplied by interpolation.
It proves that the original signal was a straight line between the measurements.
It proves that the acquisition sample rate doubled.
It is a value computed by the chosen interpolation rule, not an independently recorded sample.

items.prompt: A standard N-point DFT is computed from N = 40 uniformly spaced samples recorded at 20 samples per second. What is the spacing from the frequency-bin centre at k = 0 to the one at k = 1? This asks for bin spacing, not guaranteed separation of two tones.

A 1 Hz zero-phase cosine and a 7 Hz zero-phase cosine have identical samples at every time t = n/8 seconds. Without any additional information about the source, would extending this exact uniform recording at the same rate distinguish these two possibilities from the recorded samples alone?
options: Yes; enough extra samples always remove this exact alias.
No; the sequences agree at every integer index, including all newly recorded indices.
Yes; drawing a denser line through the samples creates the missing information.
No, because all sampled signals are indistinguishable from one another.
